claim: Non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) has a low propensity (20%) of becoming muscle-invasive (MIBC).
source: It has long been recognized that non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) has a low propensity (20%) of becoming muscle-invasive (MIBC)
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the field of bladder cancer research.

claim: MIBC carry many more p53 point mutations than NMIBC (50% vs 10%).
source: MIBC carry many more p53 point mutations (p53m) than NMIBC (50% vs 10%)
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the field of bladder cancer research.

claim: MIBC has a higher mutation burden than NMIBC.
source: MIBC also has a higher mutation burden than NMIBC
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the field of bladder cancer research.

claim: MIBC cells are hypermutable.
source: We found MIBC cells are hypermutable
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A showing higher mutation frequencies in MIBC cells.

claim: MIBC cells are deficient in DNA repair.
source: We found MIBC cells are hypermutable, deficient in DNA repair
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1B-F showing reduced DNA repair capacity in MIBC cells.

claim: MIBC cells have markedly downregulated DNA repair genes XPC, hOGG1/2 and Ref1.
source: We found MIBC cells are hypermutable, deficient in DNA repair and have markedly downregulated DNA repair genes, XPC, hOGG1/2 and Ref1
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3 showing expression levels of these genes.

claim: MIBC cells have markedly downregulated the tumor suppressor TAp63γ.
source: We found MIBC cells are hypermutable, deficient in DNA repair and have markedly downregulated DNA repair genes, XPC, hOGG1/2 and Ref1, and the tumor suppressor, TAp63γ
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A showing p63 protein expression.

claim: NMIBC cells are hyperactive in DNA repair.
source: In contrast, NMIBC cells are hyperactive in DNA repair
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1B-F showing enhanced DNA repair capacity in NMIBC cells.

claim: NMIBC cells exhibit upregulated DNA repair genes and TAp63γ.
source: In contrast, NMIBC cells are hyperactive in DNA repair and exhibit upregulated DNA repair genes and TAp63γ
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2A and 3 showing expression levels.

claim: MIBC tissues have markedly lower DNA repair activity compared to NMIBC tissues.
source: A parallel exists in human tumors, as MIBC tissues have markedly lower DNA repair activity, and lower expression of DNA repair genes and TAp63γ compared to NMIBC tissues
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5 showing DNA repair capacity in human tumor tissues.

claim: MIBC tissues have lower expression of DNA repair genes compared to NMIBC tissues.
source: A parallel exists in human tumors, as MIBC tissues have markedly lower DNA repair activity, and lower expression of DNA repair genes and TAp63γ compared to NMIBC tissues
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5C-D showing protein expression in human tumor tissues.

claim: MIBC tissues have lower expression of TAp63γ compared to NMIBC tissues.
source: A parallel exists in human tumors, as MIBC tissues have markedly lower DNA repair activity, and lower expression of DNA repair genes and TAp63γ compared to NMIBC tissues
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5C-D showing p63 protein expression in human tumor tissues.

claim: Forced TAp63γ expression in MIBC significantly mitigates DNA repair deficiencies.
source: Forced TAp63γ expression in MIBC significantly mitigates DNA repair deficiencies
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2C showing enhanced DNA repair capacity upon TAp63γ transfection.

claim: Forced TAp63γ expression in MIBC reduces mutational susceptibility.
source: Forced TAp63γ expression in MIBC significantly mitigates DNA repair deficiencies and reduces mutational susceptibility
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2D showing reduced mutation frequency upon TAp63γ transfection.

claim: Knockdown of TAp63γ in NMIBC greatly reduces DNA repair capacity.
source: Knockdown of TAp63γ in NMIBC greatly reduces DNA repair capacity
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2E showing reduced DNA repair capacity upon TAp63γ knockdown.

claim: Knockdown of TAp63γ in NMIBC enhances mutational susceptibility.
source: Knockdown of TAp63γ in NMIBC greatly reduces DNA repair capacity and enhances mutational susceptibility
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2F showing increased mutation frequency upon TAp63γ knockdown.

claim: Manipulated TAp63γ expression reduces the invasion of MIBC by 40–60%.
source: Manipulated TAp63γ expression or knockdown of p53m reduce the invasion of MIBC by 40–60%
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A showing reduced invasion potential upon TAp63γ expression.

claim: Knockdown of p53m reduces the invasion of MIBC by 40–60%.
source: Manipulated TAp63γ expression or knockdown of p53m reduce the invasion of MIBC by 40–60%
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A showing reduced invasion potential upon p53 knockdown.

claim: The combination of p53m knockdown with forced TAp63γ expression reduces the invasion ability of MIBC to nil.
source: However, the combination of p53m knockdown with forced TAp63γ expression reduce the invasion ability to nil
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A showing nearly complete loss of invasion potential with combined treatment.

claim: p53m contributes to invasion phenotype independent from TAp63γ.
source: However, the combination of p53m knockdown with forced TAp63γ expression reduce the invasion ability to nil suggesting that p53m contributes to invasion phenotype independent from TAp63γ
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the experimental data showing additive effects of p53m knockdown and TAp63γ expression.

claim: In BC, TAp63γ regulates DNA repair capacities.
source: These results indicate that in BC, TAp63γ regulates DNA repair capacities, mutational susceptibility and invasion
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2 and 3 showing effects of TAp63γ manipulation on DNA repair.

claim: In BC, TAp63γ regulates mutational susceptibility.
source: These results indicate that in BC, TAp63γ regulates DNA repair capacities, mutational susceptibility and invasion
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2D and 2F showing effects of TAp63γ manipulation on mutation frequency.

claim: In BC, TAp63γ regulates invasion.
source: These results indicate that in BC, TAp63γ regulates DNA repair capacities, mutational susceptibility and invasion
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4 showing effects of TAp63γ manipulation on invasion potential.

claim: p53m contribute to the invasion phenotype in BC.
source: These results indicate that in BC, TAp63γ regulates DNA repair capacities, mutational susceptibility and invasion, and that p53m contribute to the invasion phenotype
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4 showing effects of p53 knockdown on invasion potential.

claim: Concurrent TAp63γ suppression and acquisition of p53m are a major cause for MIBC development.
source: We conclude that concurrent TAp63γ suppression and acquisition of p53m are a major cause for MIBC development
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing the combined effects of TAp63γ and p53m on DNA repair, mutation, and invasion.

claim: NMIBC are low-grade papillary types that are well- to moderately-differentiated and do not penetrate the lamina propria of the bladder wall.
source: There are two major forms of BC: the low-grade papillary types that are well- to moderately-differentiated and do not penetrate the lamina propria of the bladder wall (non-muscle-invasive BC, NMIBC), and the muscle-invasive types (MIBC) that are much more poorly differentiated (Wu, 2005; Van Batavia et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wu, 2005 and Van Batavia et al., 2014.

claim: MIBC are much more poorly differentiated than NMIBC.
source: There are two major forms of BC: the low-grade papillary types that are well- to moderately-differentiated and do not penetrate the lamina propria of the bladder wall (non-muscle-invasive BC, NMIBC), and the muscle-invasive types (MIBC) that are much more poorly differentiated (Wu, 2005; Van Batavia et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wu, 2005 and Van Batavia et al., 2014.

claim: NMIBC is much less malignant and less lethal than MIBC.
source: While the former is much less malignant and less lethal than the latter, it frequently recurs after surgery

claim: NMIBC frequently recurs after surgery.
source: While the former is much less malignant and less lethal than the latter, it frequently recurs after surgery

claim: The molecular paths that lead to NMIBC and MIBC are unclear.

claim: Most, if not all, tumor cells have the propensity of malignant progression.

claim: Only 20% of NMIBC progress into MIBC.

claim: High-grade MIBC have a much higher genomic DNA mutation burden than low-grade NMIBC.

claim: UVC-DNA damage induces two- to eightfold more mutations in MIBC cells than in NMIBC cells or UROtsa cells.

claim: ODD induces six- to eightfold more mutations in MIBC cells compared to NMIBC cells or UROtsa cells.
source: The results in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1 show that UVC-DNA damage induces two- to eightfold more mutations in MIBC cells than in NMIBC cells or UROtsa cells, and that ODD induces six- to eightfold more mutations in MIBC cells compared to NMIBC cells or UROtsa cells
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The susceptibility to DNA-damage-induced mutagenesis of NMIBC cells and UROtsa cells is similar to that of other cultured human cells such as normal lung fibroblasts and skin fibroblasts.

claim: Compared to NMIBC and normal human cells, MIBC cells are hypermutable.

claim: H2O2-induced ODDs disappear (are repaired) within 24 hr incubation in NMIBC cells.
source: Results in Figure 1B and C show that, whereas UV-induced CPDs (T4 endo V sensitive sites) and H2O2-induced ODDs (Fpg sensitive sites) disappear (repaired) within 24 hr incubation in NMIBC cells, these DNA damages remain in MIBC cells

claim: UV-induced CPDs remain in MIBC cells after 24 hr incubation.

claim: The major repair pathways for bulky CPDs and ODDs are NER and BER mechanisms.

evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about DNA repair mechanisms.

claim: NMIBC cells are proficient in NER and BER.
source: Since it is well established that the major repair pathways for bulky CPDs and ODDs are NER and BER mechanisms, these results indicate that NMIBC cells are proficient in NER and BER, whereas MIBC cells are deficient in NER and BER

claim: MIBC cells are deficient in NER and BER.

claim: NMIBC and UROtsa cells have hyperactive NER and BER functions.

claim: XPC, Ref1, and hOGG1/2 are highly expressed in NMIBC cells but are either not or lowly expressed in MIBC cells.

claim: Transfection-induced TAp63γ expression elevates levels of XPC, Ref1, and hOGG1/2 in MIBC cells.

claim: Knockdown of TAp63γ expression causes a downregulation of XPC, Ref1, and hOGG1/2 in NMIBC cells.
